youtube.baslik: Bilateral Fitting, CROS and BiCROS | Lesson 194 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Why are two hearing aids usually preferred, and what can we offer someone who cannot benefit from one ear? In this lesson we cover binaural advantages, late-onset auditory deprivation, binaural interference, CROS and BiCROS systems, and other options for single-sided deafness.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Silman, Gelfand and Silverman (1984), Late-onset auditory deprivation: effects of monaural versus binaural hearing aids, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; Jerger, Silman, Lew and Chmiel (1993), Case studies in binaural interference, Journal of the American Academy of Audiology; Mueller, Ricketts and Bentler, Modern Hearing Aids.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn why fitting both ears is usually preferred, and about late-onset auditory deprivation.

cumleler.yazi: Then we will look at CROS and BiCROS systems, which route sound to the other side for people who cannot benefit from one ear.
cumleler.ses: Then we will look at CROS and bye cross systems, which route sound to the other side for people who cannot benefit from one ear.

ogeler.metin: The ear on the better side

cumleler: Binaural amplification aims to preserve the advantages of binaural hearing.
Through binaural summation, a sound seems louder with two ears; about 3 dB at threshold and about 6 dB above threshold are reported.
Thanks to the head shadow effect, the person can make use of the ear on the side away from the noise.
Binaural squelch uses the time and level differences reaching the two ears to help separate speech from noise.
Localization also depends on these differences between the ears; with a single aid, these cues are distorted.
Users often say that with two aids, sound is fuller, more balanced and more natural.
In this drawing, speech comes from one side and noise from the other.
In the ear in the head's shadow, noise is reduced; the signal-to-noise ratio is better in this ear.
A person fitted in both ears can use whichever ear is better placed, whatever side the speech and noise come from.
In a person using a single aid, however, the better-placed ear may be unaided, and this advantage is lost.
This is why two aids are usually recommended for people with bilateral losses of similar degree.
Also, the two aids can communicate wirelessly and change programs and volume together.

maddeler.metin: Slightly less gain in each aid

cumleler: Because the two ears add up loudness, slightly less gain in each aid is enough for the same loudness with two aids.

cumleler.yazi: This is why formulas such as NAL-NL2 give lower targets for bilateral fittings than for unilateral ones.

cumleler: Less gain can also have a positive effect on sound quality and comfort.
In addition, the margin before feedback increases; this is especially important in open fittings.
For the target to be calculated correctly, the fact that the fitting is bilateral must be entered in the software.
In some people with bilateral loss who are fitted in only one ear, an interesting change is seen.
This graph shows the change with example values: the speech discrimination score of the aided ear stays stable over the years.
The score of the unaided ear, however, declines over time, even though the thresholds of both ears have not changed.
This is called late-onset auditory deprivation.

cumleler.yazi: It was first described in 1984, in a study comparing people who used one hearing aid and two hearing aids.
cumleler.ses: It was first described in nineteen eighty-four, in a study comparing people who used one hearing aid and two hearing aids.

cumleler: When the unaided ear is later fitted, the score partly recovers in some people but not in others.
In some people, mostly at an older age, listening with two ears can give a worse result than listening with one.

cumleler.yazi: This is called binaural interference; it was described in case studies in the 1990s.
cumleler.ses: This is called binaural interference; it was described in case studies in the nineteen nineties.

cumleler: If the difference between the ears is very large and one ear cannot gain meaningful benefit from an aid, two aids may lose their point.
Dexterity or cost can make using two aids difficult; this is also part of the decision.
If in doubt, the person tries both one and two aids for a while in their own settings, and the decision follows that experience.
For most people, though, two aids give better results both in measurements and in the person's own assessment.
In this example, the right ear is within normal limits.
The left ear, on masked testing, has a profound loss; at high frequencies there is no response at the limits of the audiometer.
In such an ear the speech discrimination score is also usually very low; the ear cannot gain meaningful benefit from amplified sound.
This is called single-sided deafness.
The person hears well in quiet, but struggles markedly when spoken to from the left and in noise.
Children with unilateral loss also have a higher risk of difficulties at school, so they are monitored closely as well.
Contralateral routing of signals, or CROS, is a system developed for this problem.
A device containing only a microphone and transmitter is fitted on the poor ear.
This device picks up sound on the poor side and sends it wirelessly to the receiving device on the good ear.
This way the person hears sound from the poor side with the good ear; the head shadow is no longer a barrier.
Because the good ear is normal, the device there is usually fitted with an open tip and does not occlude the ear canal.
So CROS does not improve the poor ear; it only carries sound from that side to the good ear.
Today this transfer is wireless; in older systems the two devices were connected by a cable behind the head.
The biggest benefit of CROS is that speech from the poor side, for example a passenger in the car, can be heard.
However, because two-eared hearing does not return, localization and binaural squelch do not improve.
If noise comes from the poor side, CROS carries this noise to the good ear too, and can make understanding speech harder.
This is why many systems allow the transmitter to be switched on and off, or a directional microphone to be used.
The person's benefit depends largely on their daily settings; the decision is made after a trial period in real life.
The user should be told clearly that the system targets not the poor ear, but the sound on its side.

sahneler.baslik: *BiCROS*: loss in the better ear too
cumleler: In this example the left ear again cannot benefit, but this time the right ear also has a mild to moderate loss.
The right ear itself also needs amplification.

cumleler.yazi: BiCROS means bilateral CROS: the aid on the better ear amplifies both the sound at its own microphone and the sound from the other side.
cumleler.ses: Bye cross means bilateral CROS: the aid on the better ear amplifies both the sound at its own microphone and the sound from the other side.

cumleler: So the aid on the better ear is fitted and verified to a prescriptive target based on that ear's loss.
How much the ear canal is occluded is also chosen according to the degree of loss in the better ear.
Now let us see the options together.
For a bilateral loss of similar degree, two hearing aids are usually recommended.
If one ear cannot benefit from an aid and the other ear is normal, CROS can be considered.

cumleler.yazi: If the ear opposite the unaidable ear also has a loss, BiCROS becomes an option.
cumleler.ses: If the ear opposite the unaidable ear also has a loss, bye cross becomes an option.

cumleler: For single-sided deafness, bone-anchored devices and cochlear implants are also among the options.
With these options, the decision is made through a team assessment involving the audiologist, the physician and the person.

maddeler.metin: Via bone to the opposite cochlea
Cochlear implant: stimulates the poor ear

cumleler: Bone-anchored devices transmit sound from the poor side to the cochlea on the good side through skull vibration.
Like CROS, this carries sound to the other side, but the sound arrives through bone rather than air.
In single-sided deafness, a cochlear implant stimulates the poor ear itself and aims to partly restore hearing with two ears.
For this option, factors such as the duration of deafness and the state of the auditory nerve are assessed by the team.
Each option has its own advantages; the audiologist's job is to explain them to the person impartially.

sahneler.metin: Ask a person about to try CROS which side noise usually comes from. Daily situations such as the car, the table and seating at work decide its benefit.
cumleler: A tip from the field: before recommending CROS, ask in detail about the person's daily settings.
Which seat do they sit in in the car, where at the table in meetings, and which side does noise come from at work?
If talkers are often on the poor side, the benefit can be large; if the poor side is always noisy, it may stay limited.
During the trial period, ask the person to keep short notes about these situations.
At the follow-up visit, these notes make the decision to continue with the system or move to another option concrete.

maddeler.metin: Two ears: summation, shadow, squelch, localization
With one aid, the unaided ear may decline
CROS: poor-side sound to the good ear
BiCROS: when the better ear has loss

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that two aids preserve the advantages of binaural summation, head shadow, squelch and localization.
In people with bilateral loss who use one aid, late-onset auditory deprivation can be seen in the unaided ear.
CROS carries sound from the side of the unaidable ear to the good ear, but does not restore localization.

cumleler.yazi: BiCROS, when the better ear also has a loss, amplifies that ear while adding the sound from the other side.
cumleler.ses: Bye cross, when the better ear also has a loss, amplifies that ear while adding the sound from the other side.

sahneler.soru: One ear is unaidable and the other has a moderate loss. Which?
secenekler: One aid on the poor ear
sahneler.aciklama: Because the better ear also needs amplification, _BiCROS_ both amplifies that ear and adds the sound from the other side.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which system suits a person who cannot benefit from an aid in one ear and has a moderate loss in the other?
The correct answer is C: BiCROS.
cumleler.ses: The correct answer is C: bye cross.

cumleler: Because the better ear also needs amplification, the system both amplifies that ear and adds the sound from the other side to it.
